sections.title: Metallic bonding and metal properties
sections.summary: Mobile electrons attract a lattice of metal cations.
explain: In a metal, outer electrons are delocalized across an extended structure rather than confined to one bond. Electrostatic attraction between these electrons and positive metal ions holds the solid together.

Mobile electrons transport charge and energy, explaining electrical and thermal conductivity. Metallic attraction is non-directional, so layers can move while attraction to the electron cloud remains; this explains malleability.
steps: Identify cations and delocalized electrons
For conductivity, identify mobile electrons
For malleability, explain maintained attraction as layers move

example.q: Why can a metal be hammered into shape without shattering like an ionic crystal?
steps: Metal ions can change relative positions under force
Electrons remain delocalized across the structure
Electrostatic attraction is maintained rather than creating strongly repelling like-charge planes

sections.mistake: Do not say positive metal ions conduct electricity by moving through a solid wire.

sections.title: What strengthens metallic bonding?
sections.summary: Greater cation charge and smaller radius usually strengthen metallic attraction.
explain: Metallic bonding depends on how strongly the cations attract the delocalized electrons. A greater positive charge and a smaller ionic radius increase this attraction, provided comparable structures are being considered.

Across the period-3 metals sodium, magnesium and aluminium, increasing numbers of contributed electrons and higher cation charge generally strengthen metallic bonding. More energy is required to overcome the stronger attractions, giving higher melting points in this simple comparison.
steps: Compare cation charges
Compare radii and electron density
Relate attraction strength to melting point

example.q: Explain the general increase in melting point from Na to Mg to Al.
steps: Na contributes one outer electron, Mg two and Al three in the simple model
Cation charge increases while size generally decreases
The denser electron cloud and stronger attraction require more energy to overcome
example.answer: Metallic bonding generally strengthens from Na to Al.

sections.mistake: Do not describe a metal as separate molecules joined by intermolecular forces.

sections.title: Transition-metal bonding
sections.summary: Delocalized d electrons contribute to transition-metal properties.
explain: Transition elements can involve d electrons as well as outer s electrons in metallic bonding. Their delocalized electron population can produce strong attractions to the positive ion framework.

This helps explain their typically high melting temperatures and good electrical conductivity. Melting trends across the d block are less simple than the s-block model because electron arrangements and solid structures vary.
steps: Identify available delocalized d and s electrons
Connect stronger attraction to melting temperature
Connect mobile electrons to conductivity

example.q: Why is iron generally a high-melting electrical conductor?
steps: Its solid contains metallic bonding with delocalized electrons
Strong attraction throughout the lattice requires substantial energy to overcome
Mobile delocalized electrons carry charge
example.answer: Strong metallic bonding and mobile electrons explain the properties.

sections.mistake: Avoid claiming every transition element has a higher melting point than every main-group metal.

sections.title: The bonding continuum
sections.summary: Ionic, covalent and metallic descriptions are useful limiting models.
explain: Real bonding does not always fit into three completely separate boxes. Some substances combine unequal electron sharing, directional covalent character and more widespread electron delocalization. A bonding triangle represents this continuum.

Use the dominant bonding contribution to explain observed behaviour, while recognizing mixed character. A material near an ionic region may have high melting temperature and conduct when molten; a material with metallic character is more likely to conduct as a solid.
steps: Identify observed properties
Choose the most useful bonding model
State where mixed character limits a simple classification

example.q: Why is a bonding continuum more useful than insisting every compound is perfectly ionic or covalent?
steps: Electron sharing varies continuously with the atoms involved
Many real bonds have mixed character
A continuum helps connect this mixture to measured physical properties
example.answer: Bonding models are limits, not perfectly separated categories.

sections.mistake: A triangle position is a model of bonding character, not a claim that a sample contains three separate phases.

sections.title: Using electronegativity in a bonding triangle
sections.summary: Electronegativity difference and average locate binary substances in a bonding model.
explain: For a binary compound, calculate the electronegativity difference Δχ = |χA − χB| and the average χaverage = (χA + χB)/2. Use these values with the axes and regions of the supplied bonding triangle.

A large difference usually suggests substantial ionic character. A small difference combined with a high average suggests shared electrons in covalent bonding; a small difference and low average is associated with metallic character. These are tendencies, not universal rules.
steps: Look up both electronegativities
Calculate difference and average
Plot using the supplied axes and infer properties

example.q: For atoms with χ = 0.9 and 3.0, calculate the coordinates used with a bonding triangle.
steps: Difference =
Use the supplied triangle; the relatively large difference suggests ionic character

sections.mistake: Do not calculate percentage ionic character; the syllabus does not require it.

visual.title: Using electronegativity in a bonding triangle

sections.title: Alloys and enhanced properties
sections.summary: Alloys are mixtures with modified metallic structures and useful properties.
explain: An alloy contains a metal mixed with one or more other elements. Differently sized atoms can disrupt the regular arrangement of a pure metal, making it harder for layers or defects to move. This often increases hardness.

Metallic bonding remains non-directional, allowing mixtures without needing a fixed molecular ratio. Alloy composition can be selected for strength, corrosion resistance or other properties; examples include brass, bronze and stainless steel, but specific recipes need not be memorized.
steps: Identify the base metal and mixed atoms
Explain disruption of a regular lattice
Relate restricted sliding to hardness

example.q: Why can an alloy be harder than a pure metal?
steps: Added atoms can differ in size
They distort the regular metal arrangement
Movement of layers becomes more difficult while metallic attraction remains

sections.mistake: Alloys are mixtures, not necessarily compounds with fixed formulas.

sections.title: Polymer structure and plastic properties
sections.summary: Polymers are macromolecules built from repeated monomer units.
explain: A polymer is a very large molecule constructed from many repeated subunits. Long covalently bonded chains may become entangled, and attractions between chains help determine flexibility, strength and softening behaviour.

Many plastics are lightweight, mouldable and poor electrical conductors because they lack mobile charge carriers. Natural polymers and synthetic polymers share the repeated-unit idea, although their functional groups and chain structures differ considerably.
steps: Identify the repeated structural pattern
Distinguish covalent chain bonds from attractions between chains
Connect chain arrangement to a stated property

example.q: Why can a common polymer plastic be a useful electrical insulator?
steps: Its electrons are largely localized in covalent bonds
It lacks mobile ions in the solid
There are no abundant mobile charge carriers to transport current
example.answer: A lack of mobile charge carriers explains insulation.

sections.mistake: Do not say all polymers are identical or all are biodegradable.

sections.title: Addition polymerization
sections.summary: Alkene double bonds open to connect monomers without eliminating a small molecule.
explain: In addition polymerization, the carbon–carbon double bond in each alkene monomer becomes a carbon–carbon single bond as new bonds form to neighbouring units. The polymer backbone contains the two original alkene carbons.

Draw one repeat unit in brackets with continuation bonds passing through both sides and n outside. All monomer atoms remain in the polymer, so the ideal addition process has 100% atom economy. Side groups stay attached to their original carbon.
steps: Identify the C=C bond
Change it to a C–C backbone and retain side groups
Add continuation bonds, brackets and n

example.q: Write the repeat unit formed from propene, CH2=CHCH3.
steps: The two double-bond carbons become the backbone
Retain CH3 attached to the second backbone carbon
Represent one repeat unit with open continuation bonds

sections.mistake: Do not include the original C=C bond inside a simple alkene addition-polymer repeat unit.

sections.title: Condensation polymers
sections.summary: Functional groups join monomers while releasing a small molecule.
explain: Condensation polymerization joins monomers with suitable functional groups at two sites. A carboxylic acid plus alcohol forms an ester link, while a carboxylic acid plus amine forms an amide link; water is commonly released.

Polyesters contain –COO– links and polyamides contain –CONH– links. Identify the small molecule removed at each link and preserve the rest of each monomer in the repeat unit. Hydrolysis reverses these link-forming reactions and can break the chain.
steps: Identify two reactive groups on each monomer
Remove the atoms forming water at each link
Join through ester or amide links and draw continuation bonds

example.q: What link forms between a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine?
steps: A –COOH group reacts with a –NH2 group
OH from acid and H from amine form water
The remaining fragments join as –CO–NH–
example.answer: A polyamide link, –CONH–, with water eliminated.

sections.mistake: Do not confuse an amide link with an amine group: an amide contains a carbonyl beside N.

name: The periodic table: Classification of elements

sections.title: Periods, groups and blocks
sections.summary: The periodic table arranges elements by atomic number and electronic structure.
explain: Rows are periods and columns are groups, numbered 1–18. The s, p, d and f blocks reflect the types of sublevel being filled across those regions. Metals mostly occupy the left and centre, while non-metals are concentrated on the upper right.

Metalloids occupy parts of the boundary region between typical metals and non-metals and show intermediate properties. Use the data-booklet periodic table to locate elements instead of trying to infer every property from a single category.
steps: Locate the element by atomic number
Read its row and column
Identify block and broad metal/non-metal region

example.q: Where is chlorine (Z = 17) located?
steps: Find atomic number 17
It is in the third row and group 17
Its differentiating electron enters a p sublevel

sections.mistake: Group and period are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Position and electron configuration
sections.summary: Period and group information connects to occupied shells and valence electrons.
explain: The period usually identifies the highest occupied principal energy level in an atom. For main-group atoms, group membership is related to the outer s and p electron count, explaining similar chemical behaviour within a group.

Use configurations up to Z = 36 to connect electronic structure with table position. Recognize group 1 alkali metals, group 17 halogens, group 18 noble gases and the d-block transition region. Electron configuration gives a stronger explanation than simply learning group labels.
steps: Write the configuration
Identify the highest occupied n
Count outer-shell electrons for main-group placement

example.q: Deduce the position of an atom with configuration [Ne]3s2 3p4.
steps: Highest occupied principal shell is n = 3
The outer shell has 2 + 4 = 6 electrons
A p-block atom with six valence electrons is in group 16

sections.mistake: For d-block atoms, group placement cannot be determined by treating outer s electrons alone like a main-group rule.

sections.title: Periodic trends
sections.summary: Radius and electronic attraction explain recurring property patterns.
explain: Across a period, increasing nuclear charge with limited additional shielding generally reduces atomic radius and increases ionization energy and electronegativity. Down a group, added electron shells increase size and shielding, generally reducing attraction for outer electrons.

Cations are smaller than their parent atoms because electron loss can remove a shell and increases attraction per remaining electron. Anions are larger because additional electron repulsion expands the electron distribution. Electron affinity concerns the energy change when an electron is added to a gaseous atom and has exceptions; specify the sign convention used.
steps: Identify nuclear charge, shell count and shielding
Use these to compare attraction to outer electrons
Apply the reasoning to the requested property and note relevant exceptions

example.q: Why is Na+ much smaller than Na?
steps: Neutral Na has an electron in the third shell
Na+ has lost this outer electron and has only occupied first and second shells
The remaining electrons are attracted by the same nucleus
example.answer: Loss of the outer occupied shell produces a much smaller cation.

sections.mistake: Never explain a trend only with “it wants a full shell”; discuss electrostatic attraction.

sections.title: Group 1 and group 17 reactivity
sections.summary: Metal electron loss and halogen electron gain change systematically down groups.
explain: Group 1 metals react with water to form a metal hydroxide and hydrogen. Down the group, outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so electron loss becomes easier and reactions become more vigorous.

Halogens act as oxidizing agents by accepting electrons. Down group 17, increased radius and shielding make electron gain less favourable, so oxidizing strength decreases. A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from its halide solution.
steps: For group 1, write metal + water → hydroxide + hydrogen
For halogens, compare positions in group 17
Predict displacement only when the free halogen is a stronger oxidant

example.q: Predict whether chlorine reacts with bromide ions and write the ionic equation.
steps: Chlorine is above bromine in group 17
Chlorine is the stronger oxidant and accepts electrons from Br−
Balance atoms and charge

sections.mistake: Do not apply the group-1 reactivity trend to halogens; their electron-transfer roles differ.

sections.title: Oxide acidity and environmental effects
sections.summary: Oxides range from basic through amphoteric to acidic across a period.
explain: Typical metal oxides are basic and react with acids; some react with water to form hydroxides. Many non-metal oxides are acidic and react with water to form acids or with bases to form salts. Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases.

Examples include Na2O + H2O → 2NaOH, CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2, CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 and SO2 + H2O ⇌ H2SO3. Atmospheric sulfur and nitrogen oxides contribute to acid rain; dissolved CO2 shifts ocean carbonate equilibria toward greater acidity.
steps: Identify whether the oxide is predominantly metal or non-metal
Classify as basic, amphoteric or acidic using evidence
Write a balanced reaction with water where appropriate

example.q: Write the reaction of sodium oxide with water and classify the product.
steps: Sodium oxide is a basic metal oxide
It forms aqueous sodium hydroxide
Balance Na using coefficient 2 for NaOH

sections.mistake: Not every metal oxide reacts rapidly with water, even when it is classified as basic.

sections.title: Oxidation states
sections.summary: Oxidation state is a formal electron-allocation number, not necessarily an actual charge.
explain: Assign oxidation states as if each bond were ionic, with bonding electrons allocated to the more electronegative atom. An uncombined element has oxidation state zero because no net electron allocation to a different element occurs.

The sum of oxidation states equals the total species charge. Oxygen is usually −2 but is −1 in peroxides; hydrogen is usually +1 but is −1 in metal hydrides. Use known assignments to solve for unknown values and recognize nitrate/nitrite and sulfate/sulfite names.
steps: Apply familiar element rules and exceptions
Set the sum equal to the overall charge
Solve for the unknown oxidation state

example.q: Find sulfur’s oxidation state in SO4^2−.
steps: Assign each oxygen −2
Let sulfur be x: x + 4(−2) = −2
Solve x − 8 = −2

sections.mistake: Write oxidation state as +6, not 6+; oxidation state is not the same notation as ion charge.

sections.title: Ionization-energy discontinuities
sections.summary: Sublevels and electron pairing explain small decreases in an overall increasing trend.
explain: Across a period, the overall increase in first ionization energy is interrupted when the removed electron occupies a higher-energy p sublevel instead of an s sublevel, or when it becomes paired in an already occupied orbital.

For example, the electron removed from aluminium is in 3p, at higher energy than magnesium’s removed 3s electron. Sulfur has a paired 3p electron, experiencing repulsion; phosphorus has singly occupied p orbitals. Explain the energy of the electron removed rather than invoking unexplained special stability.
steps: Compare removed-electron sublevels
Check whether it is paired
Explain how higher orbital energy or repulsion lowers removal energy

example.q: Why is IE1 of Al lower than that of Mg despite greater nuclear charge?
steps: Mg loses a 3s electron
Al loses a 3p electron
The 3p electron has higher energy and is easier to remove
example.answer: A change from s to higher-energy p removal creates the discontinuity.

sections.mistake: The guide explicitly prefers electron-energy explanations to slogans about “special stability” of half-filled shells.

sections.title: Characteristic transition-element properties
sections.summary: Incomplete d sublevels support distinctive chemical and physical behaviour.
explain: Transition elements characteristically form ions with incomplete d sublevels. Their properties include variable oxidation states, coloured compounds, complex-ion formation, catalytic activity, magnetic behaviour and often high melting points.

Do not assume every compound of every d-block element shows every property. An ion with d0 or d10 configuration may not show colour from d–d transitions. Catalysis and complex formation arise from accessible electron arrangements and interaction with other species.
steps: Identify incomplete d occupation
Name characteristic properties relevant to the question
Relate a property to electronic structure without overgeneralizing

example.q: Why might a d10 ion fail to show the usual transition-ion colour?
steps: d–d absorption needs an occupied lower d orbital and an accessible higher d orbital
A filled d10 arrangement lacks the usual available d–d transition
No ordinary visible d–d absorption is expected
example.answer: A filled d sublevel does not support the usual d–d colour mechanism.

sections.mistake: “All d-block compounds are coloured” is false.

sections.title: Transition-metal ions and oxidation states
sections.summary: Similar s/d energies permit more than one stable oxidation state.
explain: The energies associated with removing successive valence electrons in transition elements can be close enough that different numbers are lost in different compounds. The accessible s and d electrons therefore allow variable oxidation states.
When writing configurations for first-row transition ions, remove 4s electrons before 3d electrons. A neutral atom’s Aufbau filling order is not the same as the electron-removal order from its ions.
steps: Write neutral-atom configuration
Remove 4s electrons first
Remove additional electrons from 3d and recount

example.q: Give electron configurations of Fe2+ and Fe3+ from Fe = [Ar]3d6 4s2.
steps: Remove two 4s electrons for Fe2+
This leaves [Ar]3d6
Remove one further 3d electron for Fe3+

sections.mistake: Do not remove 3d electrons before 4s electrons in these cation configurations.

sections.title: Colour in transition complexes
sections.summary: Visible-light absorption can promote an electron between split d orbitals.
explain: Ligands change the energies of the metal’s d orbitals, splitting them into sets. If the energy difference matches a visible photon, absorption can promote an electron between these levels. The detailed splitting patterns for different coordination geometries are not required.

The observed colour is complementary to the absorbed colour. Use the supplied colour wheel to identify the absorbed wavelength range, then f = c/λ to calculate frequency. Remember that nanometres must become metres in SI calculations.
steps: Read the observed colour
Use the colour wheel for the complementary absorbed colour
Convert wavelength and calculate frequency if required

example.q: A complex absorbs 600 nm light. Estimate the absorbed frequency using c = 3.00 × 10^8 m s−1.
steps: Convert 600 nm to 6.00 × 10−7 m
Use f = c/λ

sections.mistake: The colour seen is generally not the colour absorbed.

name: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds

sections.title: Representations of organic molecules
sections.summary: Different formulas emphasize different information about a molecule.
explain: A molecular formula counts atoms, whereas a full structural formula shows bonds and a condensed formula groups atoms along the chain. Skeletal drawings omit carbon labels and most hydrogens attached to carbon: each unlabelled line end or vertex represents carbon.

When reading a skeletal formula, add enough hydrogen to give each neutral carbon four bonds. Show heteroatoms such as O, N and halogens explicitly. Three-dimensional models reveal spatial arrangement that flat drawings can hide.
steps: Count carbons at vertices and ends
Identify all explicit heteroatoms and multiple bonds
Complete normal carbon valence and count hydrogens

example.q: Convert CH3CH2CH2OH to a molecular formula.
steps: There are three carbon atoms
Hydrogens total 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8
There is one oxygen atom

sections.mistake: Hydrogens on O or N may be explicitly shown and must be counted separately.

sections.title: Recognizing functional groups
sections.summary: Functional groups determine characteristic patterns of reactivity.
explain: Look for distinctive atom groupings: halogeno C–X; hydroxyl –OH; carbonyl C=O; carboxyl –COOH; alkoxy –OR; amino –NH2; amido –CONH–; ester –COO–; and phenyl C6H5–. A carbonyl alone does not identify every compound class.

Saturated hydrocarbons contain only C–C single bonds; unsaturated hydrocarbons contain C=C or C≡C. Functional groups influence polarity, intermolecular forces and the types of reactions a molecule can undergo.
steps: Find heteroatoms and multiple bonds
Identify the whole local group, not one bond only
Classify the compound using its group

example.q: Identify the functional group in CH3COOCH2CH3.
steps: Locate the carbonyl C=O
The carbonyl carbon is bonded to an oxygen linked to another carbon group
The combined –COO– arrangement identifies an ester
example.answer: The molecule contains an ester functional group.

sections.mistake: An ester’s –COO– is not a carboxylic acid unless the single-bonded O is attached to H.

sections.title: Homologous series and general formulas
sections.summary: Members share a functional pattern and differ successively by CH2.
explain: A homologous series is a family with a common functional group pattern and similar chemical reactions. Successive members normally differ by a CH2 unit and have predictable general formulas. For open-chain single-functional hydrocarbons, alkanes are CnH2n+2, monoalkenes CnH2n and monoalkynes CnH2n−2.

Recognize alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, halogenoalkanes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, ethers, amines, amides and esters from their structures. Formula alone may not be sufficient because different series can share a molecular formula.
steps: Identify the functional group
Check the carbon skeleton and saturation
Use a suitable general formula with its assumptions

example.q: Which series includes CH3CH2CHO?
steps: The terminal carbon has C=O and is bonded to H
This is a terminal –CHO group
Compounds with this group are aldehydes

sections.mistake: CnH2n is not uniquely an alkene formula: cycloalkanes can have it too.

sections.title: Physical-property trends in organic families
sections.summary: Chain length and branching influence intermolecular attractions.
explain: As chain length increases within a homologous series, electron count and polarizability generally rise, increasing London dispersion forces. This usually increases boiling temperature because more energy is needed to separate molecules.

Branching often reduces the contact area between similarly sized molecules, lowering dispersion interactions and boiling temperature relative to a less-branched isomer. Melting patterns can be less regular because crystal packing also matters; functional groups add further interactions such as hydrogen bonding.
steps: Compare functional groups first
Compare chain length or molar mass
For isomers, consider branching and packing

example.q: Why does hexane usually boil at a higher temperature than butane?
steps: Both are non-polar alkanes dominated by dispersion forces
Hexane has more electrons and a larger polarizable electron cloud
Its stronger attractions require more energy to overcome
example.answer: Stronger London dispersion in the larger molecules.

sections.mistake: Do not explain boiling by breaking C–C bonds; molecules remain chemically intact.

sections.title: IUPAC naming up to six-carbon parents
sections.summary: Systematic names encode the parent chain, substituents and functional group.
explain: Choose a parent chain containing the principal functional group and any relevant multiple bond. Number to give the relevant group or unsaturation a low locant, then identify substituents and use the appropriate suffix. This syllabus requires saturated or mono-unsaturated compounds with up to six carbons in the parent chain and one type of specified group.

Examples include halogeno prefixes, –ol for alcohols, –al for aldehydes, –one for ketones and –oic acid for carboxylic acids. Repeated substituents use di-, tri-, tetra-, penta- or hexa-. Make sure names distinguish position and branching.
steps: Choose parent chain
Number for the principal group
Locate and name branches and substituents

example.q: Name CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3.
steps: The longest chain contains four carbons: butan-
Number from the end giving OH carbon 2 rather than 3
Use the alcohol suffix –ol with its locant

sections.mistake: Do not choose a longest chain that excludes the principal functional group.

visual.title: IUPAC naming up to six-carbon parents

sections.title: Structural isomers and carbon classification
sections.summary: Structural isomers share a molecular formula but differ in connectivity.
explain: Structural isomers can differ in branching, position of a functional group or the functional group itself. They contain the same numbers of each atom but connect those atoms differently, which can change both physical and chemical properties.

For alcohols and halogenoalkanes, primary/secondary/tertiary describes the number of carbon groups attached to the carbon carrying OH or halogen. For amines, it describes how many carbon groups are attached directly to nitrogen—these are related ideas but different counting locations.
steps: Check equal molecular formulas
Compare connectivity rather than orientation
Identify chain, position or functional-group isomerism

example.q: Are ethanol CH3CH2OH and methoxymethane CH3OCH3 structural isomers?
steps: Both have molecular formula C2H6O
Ethanol contains an alcohol group while methoxymethane is an ether
Their atom connectivities differ

sections.mistake: Rotating a single bond does not create a new structural isomer.

sections.title: Stereoisomers, cis–trans and chirality
sections.summary: The same connectivity can produce distinct arrangements in space.
explain: Stereoisomers have the same atom connectivity and bond multiplicities but different spatial arrangements. Restricted rotation about C=C allows cis–trans isomerism when each alkene carbon has two different substituents; rings can also restrict arrangement, including C3 and C4 cycloalkanes.

A chiral tetrahedral carbon has four different attached groups and can give non-superimposable mirror-image enantiomers. Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light oppositely and can behave differently in chiral environments. A racemic mixture contains equal amounts and has no net optical rotation. Use wedge–dash drawings; E/Z naming is not assessed.
steps: Check for restricted rotation and appropriate substituents
For chirality, look for four different groups on a tetrahedral carbon
Test whether mirror images superimpose

example.q: Why is carbon 2 in butan-2-ol chiral?
steps: Carbon 2 is tetrahedral
It is attached to H, OH, CH3 and CH2CH3
Those four groups are all different
example.answer: It is a chiral centre and can form two enantiomers.

sections.mistake: A carbon attached to two identical groups is not chiral by the four-different-groups criterion.

sections.title: Organic mass spectra and fragmentation
sections.summary: Fragment ions reveal structural features of organic molecules.
explain: The molecular ion forms when an electron is removed from a molecule without initial fragmentation. Its m/z can help identify molecular mass, provided the ion’s charge is known. Fragmentation then breaks bonds to produce smaller positive ions and neutral fragments.

Interpret prominent fragment masses using the data booklet and compare proposed structures against several peaks. A high-intensity peak represents an abundant ion, often relatively stable; the base peak is not automatically the molecular ion.
steps: Locate a possible molecular-ion peak
Use fragment m/z values to suggest groups
Check all evidence against candidate structures

example.q: A molecular ion is at m/z 46 and a prominent fragment at m/z 31. What information can this provide?
steps: For a singly charged molecular ion, relative molecular mass is about 46
A 31 fragment may be consistent with CH2OH+ using supplied fragment data
The evidence supports an alcohol candidate but is not sufficient alone to prove one structure
example.answer: Molecular mass and a possible oxygen-containing fragment narrow the candidates.

sections.mistake: Do not identify a whole molecule from one fragment peak alone.

sections.title: IR spectroscopy and bond identification
sections.summary: IR absorption probes bond vibrations and functional groups.
explain: Infrared radiation can be absorbed when its energy matches a molecular vibration that changes dipole moment. Different bonds and bonding environments absorb in characteristic wavenumber ranges, so the functional-group region of a spectrum helps identify groups.

Use the data booklet rather than relying on guessed exact numbers. A broad O–H absorption and a strong C=O absorption provide different clues. Greenhouse gases absorb outgoing terrestrial infrared in suitable vibrational modes, helping explain their influence on energy transfer through the atmosphere.
steps: Inspect broad versus sharp absorptions
Compare characteristic ranges with the data booklet
Combine presence and absence of key bands

example.q: An IR spectrum shows a strong carbonyl band and a very broad acid O–H absorption. Which group is likely?
steps: A strong C=O band identifies a carbonyl-containing structure
A broad O–H band in the carboxylic-acid region suggests acidic OH
Together these indicate –COOH

sections.mistake: Do not assume every bond absorbs all IR; the vibration must involve a dipole change.

sections.title: Proton NMR: signals, shifts and integration
sections.summary: 1H NMR distinguishes hydrogen chemical environments.
explain: Hydrogen nuclei in different electronic environments respond at different chemical shifts in a magnetic field. Chemically equivalent hydrogens give the same signal, so the number of distinct signals reveals the number of hydrogen environments.

The integration ratio indicates relative numbers of hydrogens in each environment. Chemical shift values suggest neighbouring atoms or groups; use the data booklet and combine shifts with integrals instead of interpreting one feature in isolation.
steps: Count chemically different H environments
Read relative integrations
Use chemical shifts to identify likely surroundings

example.q: Why does CH3OCH3 have one main proton environment?
steps: The two methyl groups are related by molecular symmetry
All six methyl hydrogens are chemically equivalent in the usual spectrum
Equivalent hydrogens contribute to the same signal
example.answer: One signal integrating for six hydrogens.

sections.mistake: Signal count is the number of chemical environments, not the number of hydrogen atoms.

visual.title: Proton NMR: signals, shifts and integration

sections.title: Proton NMR splitting
sections.summary: Neighbouring hydrogens split signals into characteristic multiplets.
explain: In simple first-order cases, a proton set with n equivalent neighbouring hydrogens on an adjacent carbon gives n + 1 peaks: singlet, doublet, triplet or quartet for zero, one, two or three such neighbours. Equivalent protons do not split one another.

Splitting gives local connectivity information that complements integration. Exchangeable O–H or N–H signals may behave differently and often do not follow the simple rule reliably; interpret the provided data rather than forcing every peak into it.
steps: Identify equivalent proton sets
Count adjacent equivalent H neighbours
Apply n + 1 and compare with integration

example.q: Predict the splitting of the two carbon-bound proton sets in CH3CH2Br.
steps: CH3 hydrogens have two equivalent adjacent CH2 hydrogens
They give a triplet
CH2 hydrogens have three adjacent CH3 hydrogens and give a quartet
example.answer: CH3 triplet and CH2 quartet, integration 3:2.

sections.mistake: A triplet is one signal split into three peaks, not three independent chemical environments.

sections.title: Combining analytical evidence
sections.summary: A secure structure must satisfy all available analytical data.
explain: Molecular formula, mass spectrum, IR and proton NMR each answer a different question. Molecular mass and formula constrain composition; IR suggests functional groups; NMR shows hydrogen environments, counts and neighbours; fragmentation adds structural clues.

Generate plausible candidate structures and reject those contradicting any strong observation. A good answer explains why one structure fits the complete pattern, not merely why it could produce a single peak.
steps: Establish composition and molecular mass
Identify likely functional groups from IR
Use NMR signals, integration and splitting to connect groups
Check fragments and all remaining data

example.q: A C2H6O molecule has an O–H IR band and carbon-bound NMR signals with a 3:2 integration and triplet/quartet pattern. Identify it.
steps: C2H6O allows ethanol or an ether
O–H absorption favours an alcohol
A CH3CH2 unit explains the triplet/quartet with integration 3:2

sections.mistake: A candidate that matches IR but contradicts NMR is not a valid final identification.

sections.title: System, surroundings, heat and temperature
sections.summary: Energy transfers between system and surroundings while total energy is conserved.
explain: The system is the part of the universe being studied, such as the chemicals reacting in a calorimeter. Everything else is the surroundings. Energy leaving one enters the other, so a temperature change does not mean energy has been created or destroyed.

Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; temperature measures average particle kinetic energy. Two samples can have the same temperature but different total thermal energies because they contain different amounts of matter.
steps: Define the system boundary
Identify the measured surroundings
Describe transfer and conserve total energy

example.q: A reaction warms the water around it. Where did the water’s energy come from?
steps: Define the reacting chemicals as the system
Water is part of the surroundings
Energy transferred from the system to the water
example.answer: The system lost energy while the surroundings gained it.

sections.mistake: Heat and temperature are different physical quantities.

sections.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
sections.summary: The sign of enthalpy depends on the direction of heat transfer.
explain: An exothermic reaction transfers heat from the reacting system to the surroundings; the surroundings often warm and the reaction enthalpy change is negative. An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from the surroundings, often cooling them, and has positive enthalpy change.

Always state whose temperature is measured. A thermometer in solution measures part of the surroundings relative to the chemical reaction; its warming indicates energy release by the system, not a positive reaction enthalpy.
steps: Identify whether surroundings warm or cool
Infer direction of heat transfer
Assign negative ΔH for exothermic and positive ΔH for endothermic

example.q: A reaction mixture cools from 22°C to 17°C. Classify the reaction.
steps: The measured surroundings lose thermal energy
The reaction system absorbs that energy
Energy absorption corresponds to positive enthalpy change

sections.mistake: A temperature decrease does not mean the reaction enthalpy change is negative.

sections.title: Energy profiles and relative stability
sections.summary: Product and reactant energy levels determine the sign of ΔH.
explain: An energy profile plots potential energy on the vertical axis against reaction coordinate on the horizontal axis. Exothermic reactions end with products below reactants; endothermic reactions end with products above reactants.

A lower-energy chemical arrangement is more stable relative to a higher-energy one under this simple comparison. The peak represents an energy barrier, but the overall enthalpy difference is between product and reactant levels, not between reactants and the peak.
steps: Label axes correctly
Place reactant and product energy levels
Draw ΔH from reactants to products and assign sign

example.q: Products lie 75 kJ mol−1 below reactants. What is ΔH and which side is lower in energy?
steps: Calculate final minus initial energy
The product level is 75 lower
Therefore ΔH is negative
example.answer: ΔH = −75 kJ mol−1; products are lower in energy.

sections.mistake: Reaction coordinate is not time and the peak height is not the overall enthalpy change.

sections.title: Calorimetry calculations
sections.summary: Temperature change of surroundings can reveal reaction enthalpy.
explain: A calorimeter estimates heat absorbed by a known mass using Q = mcΔT, where c is specific heat capacity. At constant pressure, reaction enthalpy per mole is estimated from ΔH = −Q/n if Q measures heat gained by the surroundings.

Use mass in grams with c in J g−1 K−1, then convert joules to kilojoules for ΔH. Heat loss, calorimeter absorption and incomplete combustion can make measured changes smaller in magnitude than theoretical predictions.
steps: Compute ΔT = final − initial
Calculate Q = mcΔT for the measured material
Divide by reacted moles, reverse sign and convert J to kJ

example.q: 50.0 g water warms by 10.0 K when 0.0250 mol reacts. Use c = 4.18 J g−1 K−1. Find ΔH.
steps: The water gains heat, so the reaction loses 2090 J

sections.mistake: Q for water and ΔH for the reacting system have opposite signs.

sections.title: Average bond enthalpy calculations
sections.summary: Breaking bonds absorbs energy; making bonds releases it.
explain: To estimate a reaction enthalpy, imagine first breaking all relevant reactant bonds and then making product bonds. Energy input is positive for bond breaking, while the energy released on formation is subtracted.

Use ΔH ≈ ΣE(bonds broken) − ΣE(bonds formed). Average bond enthalpies apply to gaseous bonds and average across different chemical environments, so estimates may differ from measured enthalpies involving particular molecules and states.
steps: Balance the equation and draw structures
Count broken and formed bonds with coefficients
Subtract total formed-bond energies from broken-bond energies

example.q: Estimate ΔH for H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl using H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243 and H–Cl 431 kJ mol−1.
steps: Bonds broken: 436 + 243 = 679 kJ mol−1
Bonds formed: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ mol−1

sections.mistake: Bond breaking never releases energy by itself; bond formation is the releasing step.

sections.title: Hess’s law
sections.summary: Enthalpy change depends on initial and final states, not the route.
explain: Hess’s law follows conservation of energy. If two routes connect the same initial and final states, their total enthalpy changes must agree; otherwise a cycle could create energy from nothing.

Manipulate known equations so their sum gives the target reaction. Reversing an equation changes the sign of ΔH; multiplying an equation multiplies ΔH by the same number. Species appearing on both sides cancel.
steps: Write the target equation
Reverse or scale known equations as necessary
Add equations and their adjusted enthalpies

example.q: If A → B has ΔH = +40 and B → C has ΔH = −90 kJ mol−1, find A → C.
steps: Add the two equations
Intermediate B cancels
Add enthalpies: +40 − 90

sections.mistake: Do not reverse a reaction without reversing its enthalpy sign.

sections.title: Standard formation and combustion enthalpies
sections.summary: Definitions fix the amount and physical states used in thermochemical equations.
explain: Standard enthalpy of formation is the change when one mole of a substance forms from its elements in their standard states. The formation enthalpy of an element in its standard state is defined as zero.

Standard enthalpy of combustion refers to complete burning of one mole of a substance in oxygen under standard conditions and states. Carefully specify phases, since formation of liquid water differs in enthalpy from formation of water vapour.
steps: Identify whether formation or combustion is requested
Use exactly one mole of the defined substance
Balance with correct standard-state elements and products

example.q: Write the formation equation for liquid water.
steps: Use elements in their standard states: H2(g) and O2(g)
Form exactly one mole H2O(l)
Balance oxygen with coefficient 1/2

sections.mistake: Formation equations may use fractional coefficients to produce one mole of product.

sections.title: Formation and combustion data in cycles
sections.summary: Hess’s law leads to useful sum formulas with opposite subtraction orders.
explain: From formation data, ΔHreaction = ΣνΔHf(products) − ΣνΔHf(reactants). Formation routes start from the same elemental reference, so subtracting reactant formation energies gives the change from reactants to products.

From combustion data, ΔHreaction = ΣνΔHc(reactants) − ΣνΔHc(products), provided both sides combust to the same final products. The order reverses because both known routes go downward toward common combustion products.
steps: Balance the target equation
Choose the correct formula and multiply by coefficients
Substitute signed values and retain units

example.q: For CO + 1/2O2 → CO2, use ΔHf(CO) = −111 and ΔHf(CO2) = −394 kJ mol−1. Find ΔH.
steps: Product formation sum = −394
Reactant sum = −111 + 0 for O2
Subtract: −394 − (−111)

sections.mistake: Do not swap the subtraction orders for formation data and combustion data.

visual.title: Formation and combustion data in cycles

sections.title: Interpreting Born–Haber cycles
sections.summary: Ionic formation is related to atomization, ionization, electron affinity and lattice changes.
explain: A Born–Haber cycle applies Hess’s law to ionic-solid formation through gaseous atoms and gaseous ions. Steps may include sublimation or atomization, bond dissociation, ionization energies, electron affinities and lattice enthalpy.

Check whether lattice enthalpy is defined for formation of a solid from gaseous ions or dissociation into gaseous ions: the signs are opposite. Divalent ions require the appropriate successive ionization energies and electron-affinity steps. The syllabus requires interpretation and calculation, not construction of a complete cycle from memory.
steps: Read each arrow and definition
Include stoichiometric multiples and successive steps
Equate total indirect route with formation enthalpy

example.q: A cycle has formation ΔH = −400, atomization total +200, IE +500 and EA −350 kJ mol−1. Find lattice formation enthalpy.
steps: Add known indirect steps: 200 + 500 − 350 = +350
Set −400 = +350 + lattice formation enthalpy
Rearrange: lattice = −400 − 350

sections.mistake: Always check the stated lattice-enthalpy direction before assigning a sign.

sections.title: Complete combustion equations
sections.summary: Combustion in sufficient oxygen commonly forms stable oxides.
explain: Reactive metals and non-metals can react with oxygen to form oxides. Complete combustion of hydrocarbons and alcohols produces carbon dioxide and water when oxygen is sufficiently available.

Balance carbon first, hydrogen second and oxygen last. Alcohol fuels already contain oxygen, so count oxygen atoms present in the fuel before deciding the oxygen coefficient. Physical states may affect subsequent thermochemical interpretation.
steps: Write expected complete-combustion products
Balance C and H
Balance O last and use whole coefficients if convenient

example.q: Balance complete combustion of ethanol, C2H5OH.
steps: Two carbon atoms require 2CO2
Six H atoms require 3H2O
Products contain 7 O atoms; ethanol supplies 1, leaving 6 from 3O2

sections.mistake: Do not ignore the oxygen already contained in an alcohol.

sections.title: Incomplete combustion
sections.summary: Insufficient oxygen can produce carbon monoxide and solid carbon.
explain: When oxygen supply is limited, carbon in an organic fuel may not oxidize fully to CO2. Products may include CO, carbon particles and mixtures of partially oxidized compounds, together with water.

Carbon monoxide is a serious toxic pollutant; soot particles can harm health and reduce combustion efficiency. Which incomplete-combustion equation is appropriate depends on the specified carbon-containing products; there is not just one universal equation.
steps: Read which products the question specifies
Balance C and H
Balance O and compare oxygen requirement with complete combustion

example.q: Balance combustion of methane producing CO and water.
steps: One carbon atom gives one CO
Four hydrogen atoms give 2H2O
Products need three O atoms per CH4; multiply all by 2

sections.mistake: Do not assume incomplete combustion always produces only soot or only CO.

sections.title: Comparing fossil fuels
sections.summary: Fuel evaluation includes energy, carbon emissions, pollution and resource limits.
explain: Coal, crude-oil fuels and natural gas release chemical energy on combustion but are non-renewable on human timescales. Compare their energy per unit mass and the quantity of CO2 produced per unit energy, not only CO2 per mole.

Larger carbon-rich fuels can have greater tendency toward incomplete combustion under poor mixing. CO2 absorbs appropriate outgoing infrared radiation and contributes to the greenhouse effect. Environmental comparisons should also consider extraction, leakage, transport and other pollutants.
steps: Balance combustion and find CO2 moles
Convert to mass or per-energy basis as required
Compare with wider environmental and practical factors

example.q: How much CO2 is produced by complete combustion of one mole of methane?
steps: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O
One mole CH4 produces one mole CO2
M(CO2) is approximately 44.01 g mol−1
example.answer: Approximately 44.01 g CO2 per mole CH4.

sections.mistake: Lower CO2 per mole of fuel is not automatically lower CO2 per kJ of useful energy.

sections.title: Biofuels and renewable carbon
sections.summary: Photosynthesis fixes carbon recently enough for biomass to replenish.
explain: Photosynthesis converts carbon dioxide and water into organic material using light energy. A simplified equation is 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2. Biofuels derive from such recently fixed biological carbon rather than ancient fossil carbon.

Biofuels may be renewable if their sources can regrow sustainably, but they are not automatically carbon-neutral. Farming, fertilizer, processing and transport use energy, while land-use change and competition with food production can be important disadvantages.
steps: Explain the source and timescale of carbon fixation
Distinguish renewable resource from zero emissions
Evaluate life-cycle benefits and costs

example.q: Why can a biofuel be renewable but still cause net greenhouse-gas emissions?
steps: Its biomass can regrow and replace harvested material
Production and transport may consume fossil energy
Land-use change may release stored carbon
example.answer: Renewability does not guarantee zero life-cycle emissions.

sections.mistake: Never call a fuel carbon-neutral solely because a plant originally absorbed CO2.

sections.title: Hydrogen and methanol fuel cells
sections.summary: Fuel cells continuously convert supplied chemical fuel into electrical energy.
explain: A fuel cell separates oxidation and reduction at electrodes so electrons can travel through an external circuit. Fresh fuel and oxidant are supplied continuously; unlike a sealed primary cell, operation can continue while reactants are provided.

In acidic conditions, hydrogen oxidation is H2 → 2H+ + 2e−, and oxygen reduction is O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O. Methanol oxidation can be written CH3OH + H2O → CO2 + 6H+ + 6e−. Half-equations depend on acidic or alkaline conditions, so follow the medium specified.
steps: Identify the supplied fuel and electrolyte conditions
Balance oxidation and oxygen-reduction half-equations
Equalize electrons and add to obtain the overall equation

example.q: Combine acidic hydrogen fuel-cell half-equations.
steps: Multiply H2 → 2H+ + 2e− by two
Add O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O
Cancel electrons and H+

sections.mistake: Fuel-cell electrodes are where electron-transfer reactions occur; electrons travel through the external circuit, not through the electrolyte.

sections.title: Entropy and dispersal
sections.summary: Entropy measures the ways matter and energy can be distributed.
explain: Entropy increases when energy and matter can be distributed among more possible arrangements. Under comparable conditions, a gas usually has greater molar entropy than a liquid, which in turn exceeds a solid. More gas particles often mean greater entropy, but detailed data provide the quantitative answer.

Calculate a standard entropy change using ΔS° = ΣνS°(products) − ΣνS°(reactants). Values are commonly in J K−1 mol−1; unlike formation enthalpy, an element’s standard molar entropy at ordinary temperature is generally not zero.
steps: Predict dispersal from phases and gas-particle counts
Multiply standard entropies by coefficients
Subtract reactant sum from product sum

example.q: For A(g) → 2B(g), S°(A) = 200 and S°(B) = 130 J K−1 mol−1. Find ΔS°.
steps: Product entropy sum = 2 × 130 = 260
Reactant sum = 200

sections.mistake: Entropy is not simply “messiness”; link it to distributions of energy and matter.

sections.title: Gibbs energy calculations
sections.summary: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS combines enthalpy and entropy effects.
explain: Gibbs energy change relates reaction enthalpy and entropy at a specified absolute temperature. Under constant temperature and pressure, it provides a criterion for thermodynamic direction. The standard form is ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°.
Match units before substituting. If ΔH is kJ mol−1 and ΔS is J K−1 mol−1, divide ΔS by 1000 before calculating TΔS. Use kelvin, never Celsius. The sign of the result is as important as the magnitude.
steps: Convert temperature to K
Put ΔH and TΔS in matching energy units
Substitute with signs and calculate

example.q: At 298 K, ΔH° = −50.0 kJ mol−1 and ΔS° = −100 J K−1 mol−1. Find ΔG°.
steps: Convert ΔS° to −0.100 kJ K−1 mol−1

sections.mistake: The minus sign in ΔH − TΔS must be applied even when ΔS is negative.

sections.title: Spontaneity and temperature thresholds
sections.summary: A negative Gibbs energy change favours forward thermodynamic change.
explain: At constant temperature and pressure, ΔG < 0 indicates a thermodynamically spontaneous forward change, while ΔG > 0 favours the reverse and ΔG = 0 indicates equilibrium. Spontaneous does not mean fast: a large activation barrier can make a favourable reaction very slow.

At a threshold temperature, set ΔG = 0, so T = ΔH/ΔS with consistent units. If ΔH and ΔS are both positive, higher temperature favours spontaneity; if both are negative, lower temperature favours it. Opposite signs give temperature-independent tendencies within the assumption of constant values.
steps: Inspect ΔH and ΔS signs
Set ΔG = 0 to calculate threshold
Test above or below the threshold using the inequality

example.q: For ΔH = +40.0 kJ mol−1 and ΔS = +100 J K−1 mol−1, above what temperature is forward change favoured?
steps: Convert ΔS to +0.100 kJ K−1 mol−1
For T > 400 K, TΔS exceeds ΔH
example.answer: Forward change is favoured above 400 K.

sections.mistake: Thermodynamic spontaneity does not guarantee an observable rapid reaction.

sections.title: Gibbs energy and equilibrium
sections.summary: Reaction composition changes ΔG until equilibrium is reached.
explain: Standard Gibbs energy ΔG° refers to standard states, but actual Gibbs energy depends on the mixture composition: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. As a forward-favoured reaction progresses, Q changes and ΔG approaches zero.

At equilibrium Q = K and ΔG = 0, giving ΔG° = −RT ln K. Thus K > 1 corresponds to negative ΔG°, while K < 1 corresponds to positive ΔG°. Use R = 8.31 J mol−1 K−1 and express ΔG° in joules if using this value.
steps: Distinguish actual ΔG from standard ΔG°
Use ΔG = 0 and Q = K at equilibrium
Calculate K or ΔG° with matching units

example.q: At 298 K, K = 10.0. Estimate ΔG° using R = 8.31 J mol−1 K−1.
steps: Use ΔG° = −RT ln K
Substitute −8.31 × 298 × ln(10.0)
This is approximately −5700 J mol−1

sections.mistake: At equilibrium actual ΔG is zero, but ΔG° need not be zero unless K = 1.
